title: Moves
summary: Assigning or passing a non-Copy value transfers ownership — the old name dies.
lecture: In Rust, every value has exactly one owner. Assigning a String, Vec, or any other non-Copy value to another binding — or passing it to a function — does not copy it. It MOVES it: ownership transfers, and the original binding becomes unusable.

This is not a runtime mechanism. The compiler simply refuses to let you touch a moved-from name, and the error is E0382: 'use of moved value'. Small scalar types (i32, bool, char, &T) are Copy, so they duplicate instead of moving — which is why this rule surprises people coming from GC languages only for heap-owning types.
When you hit E0382, the question is never 'how do I silence this?' but 'who should own this value?'. If the callee only needs to look, lend it a borrow instead of moving it.

example.caption: After the move, `name` is dead — the compiler enforces single ownership.
